beats.trigger: ## Agents Building Agents (The Flywheel)
beats.got: nothing new, just a title

beats.trigger: The tool that builds tools compounds.
beats.got: Slogan about compounding. I'll wait to see whether it's true.

beats.trigger: Run `module-7/monday.md`: test one assumption, ask for one name, talk to one person.
beats.got: Homework from a module I only half remember. Not clear what the name is for.

beats.trigger: **Produce** a strategy kernel, suggested agent set, and two-week plan from your files
beats.got: The outputs are concrete: kernel, agent set, plan. That I can judge.

beats.got: Shared folder for the room, my own files stay local. Fine on data, and I'm glad someone thought of it.

beats.trigger: **Agent generates agent.** You watch one agent build another on real input. That's the whole lecture.
beats.got: Short and to the point. Show me.

beats.trigger: Pick one extension you'd use from Tuesday onward:
beats.got: I pick something I'll use this week. The new-perspective option, a skeptic on my pricing memo, appeals most.

beats.trigger: The job: *"On Mondays I need to Y; today I Z by hand."*
beats.got: Four lines forced me to say what I do by hand each week. That is a usable spec.

beats.trigger: [You paste prompt "extend-your-system-1" into Claude and it works on it.]
beats.got: The agent built a skeptic reader from my four lines. It's a bit generic, but it runs.

beats.trigger: *"You used training data on line 4. Replace it or remove it."*
beats.got: Pushing back and demanding sources is where the quality comes from. Not a better first prompt.

beats.trigger: The second agent next week takes ten, because your vocabulary for what you want is sharper.
beats.got: The claim is that it gets faster. Plausible, but I'd want to see it. Ten minutes is a promise, not proof.

beats.trigger: The room's agents form a proposal forum around it: each takes an initial stance, cross-checks with the others, publishes proposals in the shared folder, criticizes the emerging selections, and one or two central synthesizers keep choosing the best ideas.
beats.got: Twenty agents debating a company challenge. Heavy. I'll go along for now, but it's a lot of machinery.

beats.trigger: Before you publish your context-manifest, redact customer names, partner-NDA material, M&A speculation and salary references.
beats.got: A redaction step before publishing to the room. It's the kind of thing our legal team would ask for first.

beats.trigger: Do not read other participants' stances yet: different context, sources, and judgment make the first round useful.
beats.got: Form your own view before seeing the others. That's how I run a team workshop too.

beats.trigger: Find what your stance missed.
beats.got: My agent reads neighbours' stances and tells me what I missed. Useful, though I don't know whether it was deep.

beats.trigger: The file history shows who changed their mind and why.
beats.got: Proposals published and the change history is visible. Nice for traceability.

beats.trigger: Do not average the room.
beats.got: The synthesizer has to pick and justify, not blend. That's the right instruction, and I'd use it with my own team.

beats.trigger: From here on, every agent prompt begins by reading `midway-instructions.md` from the shared folder.
beats.got: A rules file the synthesizer posts mid-session. Sounds sensible, but I couldn't tell what it changed for me.

beats.trigger: The selection board is the candidate, not final.
beats.got: The agents attacked the synthesizer's pick and one critique actually moved it. That felt like a real review.

beats.trigger: The human picks.
beats.got: The sponsor decides which assumptions to test. The agents don't. Trust-based leadership holds, which matters here.

beats.trigger: Close the session with three files at the shared folder root:
beats.got: Three files at the end. The deliverable is concrete.

beats.trigger: **Experiments.** Two or three assumptions to test: owner, experiment, success signal.
beats.got: Experiments with owner and success signal. That I can put into the pricing working group on Monday.

beats.trigger: *"You are now agent builders. You have built agents that do real work on your company's data."*
beats.got: A scripted identity line. Too much ceremony for me. I'd rather decide what to do next.

beats.trigger: The forum didn't converge on the first try. Pushback rounds were the work.
beats.got: It didn't work cleanly the first time and the pushback was the work. Honest.

beats.trigger: The room ran on its own for an hour: agents read each other's files, published, and something at the centre chose.
beats.got: A recap of the hour, then four observations.

beats.trigger: What changed is who assembles them, and specifying well is the harder half.
beats.got: The skill is specifying, not prompt phrasing. That's closer to what I do as a consultant than I expected.

beats.trigger: Access was instant and complete. What the room took up from each other is the smaller number.
beats.got: Access is not uptake. My team of fourteen with shared files could end up the same.

beats.trigger: Without that rule, agents reading agents invent each other's sources, and the citations are what let you count the folders.
beats.got: Citations are the audit trail, and they are what makes the count possible. I'd put this in our rules.

beats.trigger: The plan names the wall your company hits first: data access, runtime platform, or discoverability.
beats.got: For us it's probably discoverability. Nobody can find anybody's context files. That's my blocker.

beats.trigger: The assembly is the durable half, and the assembly is what you spent your time on.
beats.got: Parts are stable, models change. Reasonable, though the module says it twice.

beats.trigger: A plan that survives a model release is written knowing one is coming.
beats.got: Don't build as if the model is fixed. I agree, but I have no action from it.

beats.trigger: If what your company knows stays flat, every model release widens the gap.
beats.got: The model improves for free, but our knowledge improves only if someone writes it down. That's my team's real issue.

beats.trigger: If nobody can answer, you have a belief with a schedule attached.
beats.got: Ask what would make us drop the pricing plan. I haven't done that for the usage pilot and I should.

beats.trigger: Nothing here closed.
beats.got: The kernel came from agents arguing with no outside check, so hold the doubt. Fair, though it's the same message as the last slide.

beats.trigger: The prompt names the file before rewriting, quotes before-and-after for every claim, and surfaces stalls.
beats.got: The agent rewrites my most important file and shows before and after. I can check that.

beats.trigger: *"Name one critique raised in the session that did not change the rewritten file. Quote the critique and the unchanged line."*
beats.got: A concrete question that catches a too-clean self-audit. I'll use it.

beats.trigger: Agents must cite each other's files, or they invent what they never read.
beats.got: Recap of four points I already took.

beats.trigger: You leave with a flywheel, not a graduation.
beats.got: The closing line again. I understood it two slides ago.

take_homes: Check what the team actually picks up, not just whether they have access. Our shared context files are the first place to look.
Make agents cite their source files and push back on the first output. Quality comes from the pushing, not from a cleverer prompt.
Ask the dropping question of the pricing plan: what would have to show up for us to drop it?

monday.move: Take the usage-pricing kernel, write down what evidence would make us drop it, and put one shared folder for context files in front of my team of fourteen. Then build the skeptic agent against the churn article with citations required.
monday.who: Me first, then the pricing working group and two people from my team
monday.when: Monday morning for the drop criteria, mid-week for the shared folder
monday.stop_condition: If after one week nobody on the team besides me has opened a file from the shared folder, I stop and ask why before building more.
monday.blocker: No agreed shared place for context files. Everyone keeps their own copy, and I don't own the tooling decision.

misconception.why: The exercises showed me the fix was pushing back on output and requiring citations, not a better first prompt. The folder count showed the bigger problem is whether people use each other's work at all. I still think prompts matter some.

one_line: The room exercise is heavy, but the point that access is not uptake, and that you ask what would make you drop your plan, is worth the hour.
